Romer v. Evans. In May 1996, the Supreme Court ruled six to three to strike down Colorado's Amendment Two, which had prohibited all laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, establishing that laws targeting a class of people for disfavor violate equal protection and marked the Court's first major victory for LGBTQ rights at the federal level. The amendment had been approved by voters in 1992 and prohibited the state and its municipalities from enacting protections based on sexual orientation. The majority held that the amendment had the apparent aim of imposing a broad, undifferentiated disability on a single group. Kennedy's opinion stated that such a law could not be justified by any rational basis test and violated the equal protection guarantee of the Fourteenth Amendment. Amendment Two had overturned existing LGBTQ protections in Denver, Boulder, and Aspen, and sought to prevent future ones statewide. The three dissenters, including Justice Scalia, argued that the amendment was a legitimate expression of moral disapproval of homosexuality. The decision opened the door to subsequent equal protection challenges to anti-LGBTQ laws and policies. Kennedy's reasoning in Romer established a framework that would guide decisions in Lawrence v. Texas, Obergefell v. Hodges, and other major LGBTQ rights cases to come.
